Drugs & Therapies.evidence: 출처:조선일보+10 | 최신:Thu, 27 Aug 2026 12:16:03 GMT+5 | 키워드+30 | 순위:351위+2
Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: FDA Approves RAS-Targeting Drug That Doubles Pancreatic Cancer Survival - 조선일보
Drugs & Therapies.content:
A cancer drug that targets a previously "undruggable" protein and nearly doubles the survival period of patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer has received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This is the first targeted therapy to broadly block the "RAS" protein, which is mutated in most pancreatic cancer patients and drives tumor growth. It is expected to bring significant changes to the treatment of advanced pancreatic cancer, where options have been limited.
The FDA announced on August 26 (local time) that it approved "Rasonque" (component name: Daraksonship), developed by U.S. biotech firm Revolution Medicine, as a treatment for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma. The approved patient group includes adults who have previously received at least one systemic therapy or those unable to tolerate combination chemotherapy. The drug is taken as two 150 mg tablets once daily. The U.S. list price is 39,800 dollars per month, totaling approximately 478,000 dollars for a year of treatment. Actual patient costs will depend on insurance coverage.
The drug’s efficacy was confirmed in a phase 3 clinical trial involving 500 people with metastatic pancreatic cancer. Researchers divided participants into two groups: one received Daraksonship, while the other received existing chemotherapy.
Patients taking Daraksonship survived for more than 13.2 months on average after starting treatment, compared to 6.7 months in the chemotherapy group. The period during which cancer progression was suppressed was also twice as long—7.2 months versus 3.6 months.
Pancreatic cancer is notoriously difficult to treat. It is often diagnosed after spreading to other organs, and existing therapies have limited effectiveness. In particular, over 90% of patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma (the most common type, originating in the ducts that carry pancreatic juices) have mutations in the RAS gene. The protein produced by the RAS gene acts as a "switch" that sends growth signals to cells only when needed. However, mutations cause the switch to remain constantly "on," promoting cancer cell proliferation. RAS has long been considered "undruggable" because its smooth surface lacks binding sites for drugs. While previous approaches targeted other proteins to indirectly inhibit RAS, Rasonque was developed to directly target multiple activated RAS variants. The FDA recognized it as the first RAS-targeted therapy approved for pancreatic cancer.
However, the drug does not completely eliminate cancer. While survival periods increased significantly in trials, some patients experienced cancer progression over time. Side effects included rash, diarrhea, stomatitis, nausea, and fatigue.
This approval could influence treatments for other cancers. RAS mutations are found in about half of colorectal cancers and 30% of non-small cell lung cancers. Revolution Medicine is conducting clinical trials for other RAS-related cancers.

Metastatic pancreatic cancer: US approval for drug that doubles survival rates
The Food and Drug Administration has given the green light in record time to a tablet-based treatment that extends median life expectancy to 13.2 months
by
Maria Rita Montebelli
27 August 2026
Aggiungi Il Sole 24 Ore

3' min read
Translated by AI
For feedback, please contact
english@ilsole24ore.com
Versione italiana
Key points
The regulatory study presented at ASCO 2026
A performance worthy of a standing ovation
A new opportunity for patients with a difficult tumour
3' min read
Translated by AI
For feedback, please contact
english@ilsole24ore.com
Versione italiana
In May, news of the exceptionally long standing ovation that greeted the results of the RASolute 302 Phase 3 trial at the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) conference had spread around the world. And now, in record time, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted approval for daraxonrasib (Revolution Medicines Inc.), the ‘drug that extends the lives of patients with pancreatic cancer’, as several US newspapers have headlined.
Daraxonrasib, a RAS GTPase inhibitor, is the first targeted therapy to act on one of the key molecular mechanisms of pancreatic cancer: it ‘switches off’ the RAS oncogene, which for years was considered a ‘non-pharmacological’ target. The FDA has authorised its use for the treatment of adult patients with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma who have already received at least one course of chemotherapy and who are not eligible for systemic multi-agent chemotherapy.
The regulatory study presented at ASCO 2026
The efficacy of this molecule was assessed in the RASolute 302 trial (a randomised, multicentre, open-label study) involving 500 patients, half of whom were treated with daraxonrasib and the other half with a standard chemotherapy regimen chosen by their treating oncologists. The study endpoints were overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), assessed both in patients with a Ras mutation and in the general population. As an additional measure of efficacy, the ORR (Objective Response Rate) was calculated, i.e. the percentage of patients whose tumour shrinks or disappears completely following medical treatment.
Loading...
A performance worthy of a standing ovation
The results of the study showed a statistically significant improvement in patients treated with daraxonrasib. In particular, the median survival in the overall population was 13.2 months, compared with 6.7 months for patients assigned to the standard chemotherapy group (representing a 60% increase in survival); PFS was 7.2 months in the experimental arm compared with 3.6 months in the chemotherapy group (a 51 per cent increase); an ORR of 30 per cent was also observed in the daraxonrasib-treated group, compared with 11 per cent in the control arm. The adverse effects of this drug mainly affect the skin and mucous membranes (stomatitis, oral disorders); gastrointestinal effects (diarrhoea and perforation) and pulmonary effects (interstitial lung disease/pneumonia) are rarer.
No drug had ever achieved these results before. That is why the results of the RASolute 302 trial, presented at the end of May at the ASCO conference in Chicago and published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine, were met with a standing ovation and convinced the FDA to grant approval so quickly.
A new opportunity for patients with a difficult-to-treat cancer
The medicine is taken by mouth (one 300 mg tablet a day) until the disease progresses or significant side effects occur.
Loading...
“It’s a huge step forward,” says the trial’s lead author, Eileen O’Reilly, an oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Centre in New York. “ “The fact that it is administered as a tablet, once a day, also allows these patients to spend more time at home with their families, without having to go to hospital for intravenous infusion therapy.”
“The approval of daraxonrasib,” says Kyle Diamantas, who has been acting commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration since May, “offers an important new treatment option for these patients, who are suffering from a form of cancer that is extremely difficult to treat. It is our duty to provide these patients with more effective treatments as quickly as possible.”
Pancreatic adenocarcinoma has a high mortality rate: only 13 per cent of patients are still alive after five years, partly because the disease is often diagnosed at an advanced stage, as there is no screening available. In Italia, around 14,000 new cases are diagnosed each year, with the incidence being broadly the same in men and women.

Back row, from left: Sarah Wrobel, operations manager; Mary Jo Lamberti, director of sponsored research; Abby Dirks, senior data scientist; Zak Smith, assistant director of data science and analytics; Joseph DiMasi, director of economic analysis; Maria Florez, senior consultant; Jennifer Kim, research associate professor. Front row, from left: Emily Botto, former senior research analyst; Hana Do, research analyst; Madison Ford, research analyst; Kenneth Getz, executive director; Ava Feuer, former communications coordinator; and Victoria Zhang, intern.
Credit: Photo: Courtesy of the CSDD
Seated, from left: Sheila Shulman, Louis Lasagna, Kenneth Kaitin. Standing, from left: Joseph DiMasi, Marilyn Gosse, Brenda McGinnis, Toni Snow, Jeffrey Brown, Essie Mack-Pack, Mark Seibring, Peg Hewitt, Michael Manocchia.
Previous
Next
Newswise — When pharmaceutical companies want to make their clinical trials faster and more efficient, they look at data compiled by the
Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development
(CSDD). When the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) wants to know how the regulatory process affects drug development and approval times, they do the same. The U.S. Congress invites members of CSDD to testify. Clinical researchers consult publications from CSDD when designing and executing clinical trials. And when a layperson
reads an article
in the press about how much it costs to bring a new drug to market, it is CSDD that most likely provided the figure.
Since it was founded in 1976, CSDD has conducted scholarly analyses and published thousands of research articles that have helped pharmaceutical companies, regulatory agencies, and other research professionals in their ongoing efforts to improve the drug development process.
“We do large-scale empirical studies that we share as widely as possible with the drug development community,” said
Kenneth Getz
, research professor in the Public Health and Community Medicine Department at
Tufts University School of Medicine
and executive director of the center. “Our work helps the scientific and clinical research communities develop new treatments that address unmet and underserved medical needs faster and more efficiently.”
“The center has been a very reliable source of information about the trends in clinical research and how things are evolving,” said Robert Califf, a cardiologist at the Duke University School of Medicine who twice served as the commissioner of the FDA. “The information they produced was enormously helpful as the FDA thought about policy.”
Early Impacts
CSDD’s first impactful study, in the 1970s, documented that drugs were being approved in other major markets 3-7 years before the United States. At that time, for example, no beta blockers were available in the U.S. despite their widespread use in the United Kingdom for hypertension and other cardiovascular applications.
“The FDA was seen as conservative and risk averse, and that study showed that U.S. citizens were paying a price: Important and sometimes life-saving therapeutic drugs were not reaching the market in a timely manner,” said
Kenneth Kaitin
, a professor at the School of Medicine who joined CSDD in 1986 and was director from 1997-2020. Kaitin said that “drug lag” study added fuel to the demands for regulatory reform of the FDA and led to congressional hearings.
When the FDA announced in the early 1990s that the drug lag had finally disappeared, the agency cited data from CSDD. According to Kaitin, that highlighted the philosophy of the center’s founder Louis Lasagna, that scholarly research and analyses can and should play an important role in informing public debate on drug development and policy.
Louis Lasagna, a renowned physician and pioneer in the field of clinical pharmacology, founded CSDD in 1976 at the University of Rochester with the goal of documenting information relating to the development and regulation of new medicines “to raise the intellectual level of debate on questions of public policy.” Lasagna brought the center with him when he joined Tufts University as the first dean of the
Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences
in 1984.
Another impactful study came in 1979, when the center showed that the cost to bring a drug to market was $54 million. Since then, the center has periodically updated this study, with the next report due out in the fall of 2026.
In 1983, the center showed that, due to lack of commercial incentives, the pharmaceutical industry tended to focus on the development of drugs for broad indications, leaving patients with rare diseases few options and little hope. That led to the passage of the
Orphan Drug Act
, which provides regulatory and commercial incentives for companies to develop drugs for rare diseases.
The center also began a longitudinal study analyzing the success rate of drugs in clinical trials. Then, as now, the overwhelming majority of drugs and biologics fail to gain regulatory approval. “We’ve done a great deal of research helping to explain why drugs and biologics fail overall and by individual phases,” Getz said. “Many failed to demonstrate efficacy or had a poor safety profile. Others failed to enroll enough of the right patients or raised questions about clinical trial design and execution.”
Digging Deeper
Since its founding, the center focused on documenting what Getz calls macro-level issues, such as development costs and timelines. About 20 years ago, the center added a series of studies to get a clearer picture of underlying factors behind some of those big trends. “Protocol design and execution is one of the largest, if not the largest, drivers of rising costs and increasing levels of inefficiencies and longer timelines,” Getz said.
Every five years, Getz leads a study to analyze clinical trial protocols, which includes, among other things, quantifying the type and number of endpoints, procedures supporting them, and the number of data points generated. He has found that protocols are becoming ever more scientifically and operationally complex with highly customized designs requiring more elaborate and demanding logistics to administer.
“Complexity is running away from us,” he said. “In 2012, [the average protocol collected] under a million data points and today it’s more than 6 million as pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies focus on more challenging diseases, target more narrowly defined patient communities, and execute more global and more expansive clinical trial activity.”
While each clinical trial protocol is unique, Getz said it’s possible to identify common areas for improvement. “We devised a methodology to characterize certain design decisions,” he said, “and found there are a lot of areas that could be simplified.” One such area is the proliferation of procedures that don’t directly inform the primary endpoints the trial is measuring.
Including too many procedures not only takes more time and money, it can also deter potential participants. Indeed, the center is finding that recruitment and retention are increasing challenges.
Mary Jo Lamberti
, research associate professor at the School of Medicine and director of sponsored research at CSDD, hopes her work might help change that. “The more patients who can participate in trials, the more chances we have of getting treatments for some of the more difficult-to-treat diseases like Alzheimer’s disease or certain forms of cancer or rare diseases,” she said. “That’s how I became interested in this work. We identify areas of inefficiency and gather valuable benchmark data and generate insights.”
Lamberti gathers and publishes data related to recruitment and retention trends. She is seeing companies broaden their reach to include more sites and screen more potential study participants for a trial.
She also collects data on new tactics companies are using to reach and recruit patients, such as using artificial intelligence to seek potential participants through electronic health records and using chatbots to engage with participants.
Reducing Complexity and Burden
Zak Smith
, assistant director of data science and analytics at CSDD, evaluates strategies intended to streamline complex protocols, such as decentralized clinical trials (DCT). DCT refers to a collection of techniques and technologies to reduce visits to the research site, including telehealth visits, wearable data-collecting devices, mobile clinics, and allowing participants to complete procedures close to home.
“One of the things we’ve seen that can have the biggest impact on trial performance is to allow patients to get procedures or lab tests done with their primary care physician or at a local lab rather than visiting the clinical trial site,” he said. “That’s one of the easier and more straightforward ways to ease the burden on the participant’s side.”
He has also looked to see whether DCT strategies improve proportional representation in trials – that is, making sure the demographics of participants matches that of the intended population. “We saw that some DCT solutions may help improve diversity and others are associated with less,” he said. “Allowing the use of local labs was associated with increased diversity within the clinical trials.”
Smith has also developed a way to quantify how burdensome it is to participate in clinical trials. He analyzed thousands of patient surveys about the perceived burden of procedures and other common requirements of clinical trials. He uses the results to assess draft protocols that companies submit.
“We break it down into individual procedures, calculate a burden score and say, ‘Your burden is higher or lower than our benchmark,’” he said. “It always sparks some great conversations between the companies and us.”
Supporting Change
Moving forward, Getz wants the center to focus even more on data that could help organizations manage change in this era when everything seems to be moving at lightning speed, most notably AI.
To that end, he brought on
Jennifer Kim
, research associate professor at the School of Medicine, who is the first member of CSDD with a Ph.D. in behavioral science. “I came on board to look at drug development using a people-centered approach,” she said. “I’ve always been interested in understanding ways to tie the study of human behavior and organizational performance optimization, and in this case, we’re looking at optimizing drug development through human behavior.”
Kim is investigating the readiness of both organizations and individuals to respond to the changes that are happening in drug development. “We are looking at organizational changes, including how people are responding to AI being incorporated into their workflow, the resistance to that, and ways to address that resistance,” she said.
On the participant side, she’s studied how participants’ interactions with research staff influence their satisfaction with the experience and their willingness to complete the clinical trial and participate in future research. She found that those interactions carry a lot of weight. That’s significant, she said, because improving those interactions could be an easy-to-implement strategy to increase retention and even grow the population of future participants.
“We want patients of all backgrounds to have a good experience and to be able to go into their community and tell family and friends that participating in clinical trials is safe and can be life-enhancing,” she said.
While Kim’s work represents a new direction for the center, Getz said the longitudinal studies documenting cost, timelines, and success rates will continue. “Organizations follow these longitudinal studies to monitor how practices and use of solutions are impacting drug development performance,” he said. “There is no shortage of work to do there. At the same time, CSDD is moving into new domains. The drug development community started demanding more actionable and practical ways to react to insights we were offering, so we are evolving.”
No matter what the future brings, Getz remains committed to the mission. “I’m passionate about collecting hard data and evidence to inform insights,” he said. “We have amazing people at CSDD who share that same passion, and we love to watch the impact our research has on drug development strategies, practices, and performance. It’s meaningful and consequential work.”

Pharmaceutical Executive Daily: President Trump Planning New Medicaid Drug-Pricing Deals
Author(s)
Nicholas Jacobus
Osivax and GC Biopharma team up on a next-generation flu vaccine, K2 Therapeutics' Ying Huang talks through why so few drugs make it to market, and the Trump administration opens a new round of Medicaid drug pricing deals.
Advertisement
Welcome to
Pharmaceutical Executive Daily
, your quick briefing on the top news shaping the pharmaceutical and life sciences industry.
In today's
Pharmaceutical Executive Daily
, Osivax and GC Biopharma launch a long-term collaboration to combine their OVX836 and GC FLU vaccines into a single next-generation seasonal influenza shot, Ying Huang of K2 Therapeutics speaks on why so few drugs make it from the lab to FDA approval, and the Trump administration opens a new round of Most Favored Nation Medicaid drug pricing deals.
Osivax has entered a
long-term collaboration
with GC Biopharma to co-develop and commercialize a next-generation seasonal influenza vaccine combining two complementary immune approaches in a single injection. The partnership pairs Osivax's OVX836, a broad-spectrum influenza A candidate designed to drive T-cell responses against the virus's conserved nucleoprotein, with GC FLU, GC Biopharma's WHO-prequalified inactivated vaccine that induces antibody responses against hemagglutinin. Osivax gains a non-exclusive global license outside Japan and Korea, while GC Biopharma keeps exclusive South Korean rights and will supply the GC FLU component in exchange for royalties.
Pharmaceutical Executive
speaks
with Ying Huang, chief executive officer of K2 Therapeutics, on why so few drug candidates make it from the lab to market. Huang argues that the steep odds, drugs take eight to ten years and one to two billion dollars to reach approval, with only 40% of Phase I candidates advancing to Phase II, are what justify the company's strategy of licensing clinical-stage assets rather than building programs from scratch. He points to China's biotech licensing boom, deals reached $51.9 billion in 2024, as evidence of where that model is accelerating fastest.
Finally, the Trump administration
opens
a new round of voluntary Most Favored Nation drug pricing deals aimed at lowering what state Medicaid programs pay for outpatient drugs. The agreements would tie U.S. Medicaid prices to what manufacturers charge in other high-income countries, building on deals already in place with 17 drugmakers including Pfizer, Eli Lilly, and Johnson & Johnson; the companies joining this new round have not yet been named. The administration projects the broader Most Favored Nation framework could generate $529 billion in savings across U.S. drug markets over the next decade.
Thanks for listening to
Pharmaceutical Executive Daily
. For more updates and in-depth analysis, visit PharmExec.com.

Drugs & Therapies.content:
Revolution Medicines (NasdaqGS: RVMD) received FDA approval for RASONQUE (daraxonrasib), the first broad RAS targeted oral therapy for adults with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
The once daily treatment is the company’s first approved RAS(ON) inhibitor, following a pivotal Phase 3 trial that showed statistically significant and clinically meaningful survival benefits.
RASONQUE is now available by prescription in the U.S., addressing a major unmet need in metastatic pancreatic cancer care.
Readers who want more potential ideas linked to this kind of oncology and drug discovery story may want to continue on to

.
NasdaqGS:RVMD Earnings & Revenue Growth as at Aug 2026
Revolution Medicines is a US-based biotech focused on precision oncology, developing targeted therapies for cancers driven by RAS mutations, often referred to as RAS addicted cancers. The FDA approval of RASONQUE brings the company’s RAS(ON) inhibitor platform into commercial use for the first time.

Advertisement
How does RASONQUE’s approval reshape Revolution Medicines’ market opportunity in pancreatic cancer?
RASONQUE gives Revolution Medicines a commercial foothold in metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, a setting with limited treatment options and high unmet need. The label covers adults with metastatic disease who have received prior systemic therapy or are not candidates for multiagent chemotherapy, which broadens the eligible patient pool compared with mutation specific products.
Does this FDA approval change the Revolution Medicines Narrative?
This approval directly connects the RASolute 302 Phase 3 data to commercial use and supports the Narrative catalyst that multiple registrational RAS(ON) programs might convert to approved therapies over time. It also starts to test the risk that heavy operating expenses of US$1.6b to US$1.7b in 2026 will need to be balanced against how quickly new products can generate meaningful revenue.
If we take a look at the
community Narrative for Revolution Medicines
, we can see how this news fits into the bigger investment story.
What is the key milestone to watch next after the RASONQUE approval?
A practical signpost from here is how quickly prescriptions ramp following U.S. availability of once daily RASONQUE, helped by the (ON)Path support program and distribution through partners like Onco360. Early prescription trends over the next few quarters will give the first concrete read on commercial traction for Revolution Medicines’ RAS(ON) franchise.

Drugs & Therapies.content:
In a groundbreaking move, the Food and Drug Administration has approved a new drug to
treat advanced pancreatic cancer
. It’s a major win for Americans suffering from what’s long been considered the most incurable forms of cancer.
The FDA on Wednesday gave expedited approval to daraxonrasib, a
landmark pill
that’s been found to block tumor growth in more than 90% of pancreatic cancer cases.
Download the Straight Arrow app today to get the stories that matter free from manipulation, bias or agenda.™
Point phone camera here
Pancreatic cancer is the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the U.S., according to the
Hirschberg Foundation for Pancreatic Cancer Research
. It’s especially deadly because it often goes unnoticed until
symptoms start to appear in its later stages
. Unlike other cancers, there’s no routine screening.
And once it’s detected, there aren’t many effective treatments — until now.
What is daraxonrasib?
Daraxonrasib, which will be sold under the brand name Rasonque, is made by
Revolution Medicines
. It’s been approved for patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer who have already tried chemotherapy.
It first gained notoriety when
former Sen. Ben Sasse
shared a photo of himself on social media in which he was suffering side effects from the then-experimental drug.
In an
interview with The New York Times
in April, Sasse said that when he was first diagnosed, he was in a great deal of pain.
“I was in a ton of pain early on because I had some pancreatic tumors that were essentially pushing on my spinal column,” Sasse said. “The liver and pancreas are at the rib cage in the front, and they’re pushing out the back into my spine.”
Sasse said he was taking 55 milligrams of morphine a day and was “high as a kite.”
“But since then, the drug [daraxonrasib] has shrunk the tumors so much that I was willing to dial back up a little bit of pain to get a little bit of energy back and to be able to have a little more control of my nausea, et cetera,” he said at the time. “I’m down to only about 30 milligrams a day of morphine. I’d say my pain is 80 percent reduced from where I started.”
According to
Mayo Clinic
, the typical limit of oral morphine dose in a day is 20 milligrams.
Sasse also said while he’s grateful for the treatment and as of April his tumors had shrunk by about 76%, daraxonrasib is a “nasty drug.”
“It causes crazy stuff, like my body can’t grow skin and so I bleed all out of a whole bunch of parts of me that shouldn’t be bleeding,” he said.
How well does it work?
The company says that while the medicine is not a cure, it can significantly extend the lives of pancreatic cancer patients.
In a clinical trial, those taking daraxonrasib lived for a median of more than 13 months, a significant improvement over the less than seven months for those who underwent chemotherapy, according to the drugmaker. Revolution Medicines says some patients taking their twice-a-day pill during the clinical trials have even lived for years.
Revolution Medicines
The drug will go for $39,800 a month — or about $478,000 for a full year. Insurance is expected to cover most of the costs. It’s not yet clear how much patients will be responsible for.
More than 2,000 patients have already gotten early access to the drug for free through an expanded access program. Revolution Medicines says it will now transition to getting the drug covered through insurance.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: FDA approves groundbreaking new pancreatic cancer drug - MyStateline
Drugs & Therapies.content:
(
The Hill
) – The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Wednesday approved a treatment for advanced pancreatic cancer, offering new life-extending care for patients with one of the most aggressive forms of cancer.
The once-daily pill, called daraxonrasib and manufactured by
Revolution Medicines
, will be sold under the brand name Rasonque. It was approved for patients who already tried one line of therapy, or if they are not candidates for initial chemotherapy.
The drug is not a cure. But it’s the first real option for extending the life of patients diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.
Pancreatic cancer accounts for a disproportionately high share of cancer deaths, despite representing only about 3 percent of all cancer diagnoses. The aggressive disease is typically detected late, and there have been historically limited treatment options that do little to extend a patient’s life. The five-year survival rate is only about 8 percent.
“The FDA approval of Rasonque is a monumental step forward for patients with pancreatic cancer and for the oncology field,” Mark A. Goldsmith, chief executive officer and chairman of Revolution Medicines, said in a statement.
“For the first time, patients have an approved targeted medicine designed to directly inhibit the main cause of pancreatic cancer, RAS, which has been one of the most intractable disease targets since its discovery decades ago,” Goldsmith said.
Daraxonrasib attacks the underlying genetic causes of pancreatic cancer. It targets a group of proteins called RAS, which when mutated are a key driver of tumor growth in most patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
Patients with advanced pancreatic cancer who received the drug during a key clinical trial saw a median overall survival of 13 months, compared to just six months for patients who were offered standard chemotherapy.
The trial found daraxonrasib reduced the risk of death by 60 percent compared with chemotherapy.
“Today’s approval provides a critical new option for patients facing an extraordinarily difficult and historically hard-to-treat cancer. It is our fundamental duty to deliver more cures and meaningful treatments to patients as quickly as possible,” acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas said in a statement, adding that the approval was a “groundbreaking milestone.”
Revolution Medicines did not immediately announce how much it planned to charge for the drug.
The FDA granted Rasonque a priority review voucher, which is intended to help accelerate the review of therapies that address national public health priorities.
The company opened an FDA-cleared expanded access program (EAP) in May and has since distributed the drug to more than 2,000 patients through participating academic cancer centers and community oncology practices.
The most common adverse reactions in patients were rash, diarrhea, stomatitis, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, edema, decreased appetite and hemorrhage.
One of the most high-profile clinical trial participants is former Sen. Ben Sasse (R-Neb.), who
announced last December
that he had been diagnosed with Stage 4 pancreatic cancer. Sasse told The New York Times in April that he
credits the drug
with shrinking his tumors, but the cancer has likely spread to so many other parts of his body “that it’s probably just not something you can ever catch up on.”

Global Topical Drug Delivery Market to Reach $362.3 Billion by 2031, Driven by Rising Prevalence of Skin Disorders and Innovation in Non-Invasive Delivery Technologies
BCC Research LLC

5 min read
BCC Research LLC
"The market is projected to grow from $222.9 billion in 2025 to $362.3 billion by 2031 at an 8.7% CAGR, fueled by rising skin-disease prevalence and advances in microneedles, nanocarriers, smart patches, 3D-printed formulations and AI-assisted drug discovery."
Boston, Aug. 27, 2026
(GLOBE NEWSWIRE)
-- The global topical drug delivery market is projected to grow from $222.9 billion in 2025 to $362.3 billion by 2031, at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.7% from 2026 to 2031, according to the BCC Research report
Global Topical Drug Delivery Market
. This expansion reflects mounting disease burden, accelerating pharmaceutical R&D investment, and a pipeline of next-generation delivery technologies reshaping dermatological therapeutics.
Key Findings
• Market Scale and Growth Trajectory: The global topical drug delivery market is valued at $222.9 billion in 2025 and is forecast to reach $362.3 billion by 2031, at a CAGR of 8.7% (2026–2031), underpinned by surging demand for non-invasive treatment modalities and expanding regulatory approvals for novel topical formulations.
• Regional Leadership: North America holds the largest regional share at 46.5%, supported by strong OTC and prescription topical medicine adoption, robust dermatological infrastructure, and the influence of organizations such as the American Academy of Dermatology. The region accounts for 54.8% of total global pharmaceutical sales, reinforcing its commercial dominance.
• Disease Burden as a Structural Demand Driver: The scale of unmet dermatological need is substantial. Atopic dermatitis affects approximately 204 million people globally, psoriasis impacts more than 60 million, and fungal skin diseases accounted for roughly 1.73 billion cases worldwide in 2021. This persistent and growing disease burden is translating directly into sustained demand for effective topical therapies.
• Pharmaceutical R&D Investment Accelerating Innovation: Global pharmaceutical R&D spending reached nearly $288 billion in 2024, fuelling a robust pipeline of topical drug candidates. Recent regulatory milestones — including FDA approval of Zoryve topical foam for psoriasis in 2023 and the expanded Opzelura indication in 2024 — demonstrate the pipeline's commercial maturity and signal continued approvals ahead.
• Emerging Technologies Enhancing Efficacy and Adherence: The technology landscape is advancing rapidly. Microneedle-based drug delivery systems, nanoparticle formulations including lipid-polymer hybrid carriers, smart transdermal patches with stimuli-responsive release, 3D-printed topical formulations, and RNA-based topical treatments such as CosmeRNA for hair loss are collectively improving drug penetration, patient adherence, and therapeutic precision. AI-driven drug discovery collaborations — including the partnership between Almirall and Absci — and microneedle patch platforms under development by Daewoong Pharmaceutical further illustrate the sector's innovation velocity.
• Competitive Landscape: The market features a diversified group of multinational pharmaceutical and consumer health companies, including AbbVie Inc., Almirall, Bayer AG, Bausch Health Companies Inc., Galderma, Glenmark Pharmaceuticals Ltd., GSK plc, Haleon plc, Hisamitsu Pharmaceutical Co. Inc., Kenvue, LEO Pharma A/S, Sanofi, Solventum, and Teva Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd.
Story continues
Market Drivers
The topical drug delivery market is being shaped by two converging structural forces: an escalating global burden of chronic skin disease and a meaningful shift in patient and prescriber preference toward non-invasive, painless drug delivery alternatives. With hundreds of millions of patients affected by atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, and fungal skin conditions, the demand for effective, well-tolerated topical therapies is both large and durable. Simultaneously, growing aversion to injectable therapies — particularly among patients managing chronic conditions requiring long-term treatment — is driving formulators and developers toward transdermal and topical platforms that can achieve comparable systemic or local efficacy without needles.
These demand-side tailwinds are reinforced by supply-side momentum. Rising R&D expenditure is accelerating the translation of advanced delivery technologies — including nanocarriers, nanoemulsions, permeation enhancers, and AI-assisted drug discovery — into commercially viable products. Regulatory progress, while complex, is validating new entrants into the market, with recent FDA approvals demonstrating that the regulatory pathway for differentiated topical formulations is navigable for well-resourced sponsors.
Investment Considerations
Investors should view the global topical drug delivery market as a high-growth segment with durable demand fundamentals and a technology-driven expansion runway. The 8.7% CAGR through 2031 reflects not merely volume growth but a structural shift toward higher-value, technology-enhanced formulations that command premium pricing and stronger intellectual property protection. Companies best positioned to capture outsized returns include those with diversified pipelines spanning both prescription dermatology and OTC categories, as well as those investing in platform technologies such as microneedle systems, nanocarrier formulations, and AI-enabled drug discovery. Key risks include regulatory complexity surrounding nanomaterial-based and combination drug-device products — with 50% of stakeholders citing unclear guidance for nanomaterials — alongside drug development costs estimated at approximately $3.6 billion per new drug over timelines of 12 to 13 years. European market participants face additional approval friction for follow-on topical products under Article 10(3) of Directive 2001/83/EC. Regional disparities in access and commercialization remain a constraint on global revenue expansion.

Drugs & Therapies.content:
RAS-Targeting Pancreatic Cancer Drug That Doubles Survival Wins Ultra-Fast FDA Approval
Add to Google Preferred Sources
The U.S. FDA has approved Revolution Medicines' oral pancreatic cancer drug Rasonque (daraxonrasib). In a Phase 3 trial involving 500 patients with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, median overall survival reached 13.2 months—nearly double the 6.7 months seen with standard chemotherapy—while the risk of death fell by 60%. The drug represents a novel targeted therapy approach that blocks RAS proteins, long considered undruggable, by inducing binding with cyclophilin A. The FDA granted approval more than six months ahead of the review deadline and did not require confirmation of a specific RAS mutation. The 30-day supply is priced at $39,800 (approximately 55 million won). The approval is expected to accelerate development of follow-on drugs targeting KRAS G12D.
Key Elements
Revolution Medicines
Rasonque
daraxonrasib
FDA
RAS protein
KRAS mutation
zoldonrasib
setidegrasib
Brian Wolpin
Kyle Diamantas
An oral pancreatic cancer drug that blocks RAS proteins—targets long considered "undruggable" for decades—has won approval in the United States. Based on clinical results showing metastatic pancreatic cancer patients surviving nearly twice as long as with existing chemotherapy, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted ultra-fast approval, moving the review deadline up by more than six months.
On the 26th (local time), the FDA approved Rasonque (daraxonrasib), developed by the U.S. biotech company Revolution Medicines, for the treatment of metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma. The approval covers adult patients who have received at least one prior line of systemic therapy or who are unable to tolerate combination chemotherapy. The drug is taken as a once-daily pill, significantly reducing the treatment burden compared with intravenous chemotherapy.
The global Phase 3 trial RASolute 302, which served as the basis for approval, enrolled 500 patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer whose disease had progressed after prior treatment. Of these, 248 received daraxonrasib and 252 received standard chemotherapy. Median overall survival was 13.2 months in the daraxonrasib arm versus 6.7 months in the chemotherapy arm—nearly double. The risk of death was reduced by 60%, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.40.
The duration patients lived without disease progression was also roughly doubled. Median progression-free survival was 7.2 months for daraxonrasib versus 3.6 months for chemotherapy. The objective response rate—the proportion of patients whose tumors shrank by a predefined threshold—was 30% and 11%, respectively. The results were presented at the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) annual meeting in May and published in the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM).
Key Phase 3 endpoints are as follows:

Note: Median overall survival means half of patients were still alive at that time point.
What makes this drug particularly notable is that it directly targets RAS, the key protein driving pancreatic cancer growth. RAS is a family of proteins that act as "switches" regulating cell growth and division, encompassing KRAS, NRAS, and HRAS. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, RAS mutations are found in more than 90% of patients, and in this trial, 91.8% of participants had RAS G12 mutations.
The challenge has been that the RAS protein surface offers almost no pocket where a drug can bind stably. For this reason, the pharmaceutical industry spent decades regarding RAS as an "undruggable" target. Rasonque solves this problem through a workaround. The drug first binds to a cellular protein called cyclophilin A, and the resulting complex then attaches to activated RAS, blocking cancer growth signals from being transmitted downstream. Another distinguishing feature is that it is designed to broadly inhibit multiple forms of activated RAS rather than targeting only one specific mutation.
The FDA did not require confirmation of a specific RAS mutation as a condition of approval. This means the drug can be used regardless of RAS mutation test results, without a companion diagnostic test. This differs from some existing RAS-targeted therapies that are limited to patients with confirmed specific KRAS mutations. The FDA noted that this is the first approval of a new class of RAS-targeted therapy in metastatic pancreatic cancer.
The review speed was also unusual. The FDA designated Rasonque as a breakthrough therapy and orphan drug, applied priority review, and approved it more than six months ahead of the original review deadline. Dr. Angelo De Claro, director of the FDA's Oncology Center of Excellence, said the drug "demonstrated unprecedented results in an area of high unmet need." Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas also stated it represents "an important new option for patients facing a very difficult and historically hard-to-treat cancer."
Side effects were observed alongside the efficacy. In the Phase 3 trial, grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 61.8% of the daraxonrasib arm and 69.6% of the chemotherapy arm. The rates of treatment discontinuation due to treatment-related adverse events were 1.2% and 11.2%, respectively. Common side effects included rash, diarrhea, stomatitis, nausea, fatigue, vomiting, abdominal pain, edema, and decreased appetite. FDA labeling includes warnings for skin and soft tissue disorders, oral disorders, diarrhea, gastrointestinal perforation, and interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis. One patient death was attributed to drug-related pneumonitis.
The drug is priced at $39,800 (approximately 55 million won) for a 30-day supply. On an annualized basis, that amounts to $477,600 (approximately 660 million won). Actual patient out-of-pocket costs will vary depending on insurance coverage and the company's patient assistance programs. According to reports citing market research firm projections, Rasonque could generate annual sales exceeding $20 billion (approximately 27.6 trillion won) if it demonstrates efficacy in other cancers.
The approval is expected to have implications beyond pancreatic cancer for the development of other cancer therapies. RAS mutations are found not only in pancreatic cancer but also in roughly half of colorectal cancers and about 30% of non-small cell lung cancers. Revolution Medicines is conducting clinical trials to expand daraxonrasib into other tumor types, including lung cancer.
Development of follow-on RAS-targeted drugs is also accelerating. Zoldonrasib, being developed by Revolution Medicines, is an oral targeted therapy that selectively targets KRAS G12D, a mutation particularly common in pancreatic cancer among KRAS variants. No approved therapy directly targets this mutation, which is found in approximately 40% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma patients. Zoldonrasib is currently in the global Phase 3 trial RASolute 305, which has enrolled 670 patients with treatment-naïve metastatic KRAS G12D pancreatic cancer. In earlier Phase 1/2 studies, the objective response rate reached 82% when combined with modified FOLFIRINOX (mFOLFIRINOX).
Japan's Astellas Pharma is also pursuing KRAS G12D with setidegrasib (ASP3082). Astellas began dosing the first patient in a Phase 3 trial for metastatic pancreatic cancer in April. Unlike zoldonrasib, setidegrasib not only blocks the function of the KRAS G12D protein but also induces degradation of the mutant protein itself using the cell's protein disposal machinery. However, both drugs have only produced results from small early-stage trials so far, and actual survival benefit must be confirmed in Phase 3 studies.
Pancreatic cancer often has no obvious early symptoms and is frequently discovered only after it has already spread to other organs. According to the U.S. National Cancer Institute, the five-year survival rate for pancreatic cancer patients is 13.7%, and for those diagnosed after distant metastasis, it is just 3.4%. The American Cancer Society estimates that approximately 67,000 people in the United States will be newly diagnosed with pancreatic cancer this year, with more than 52,000 deaths.
Dr. Brian Wolpin, director of the Hale Family Center for Pancreatic Cancer Research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and principal investigator of the Phase 3 trial, emphasized that "Rasonque directly targets the fundamental biological mechanism of the disease" and that "it is easy to administer and places less physical burden on patients than standard chemotherapy, which requires hours of intravenous infusion." Dr. Andrew Coveler of Fred Hutch Cancer Center called it "one of the most eagerly awaited drug approvals in recent memory," adding that "while not a cure, it is a substantially improved option over existing treatments."
Meanwhile, shares of Nasdaq-listed Revolution Medicines have surged approximately 173% this year, rising from $79.02 on January 2 to $215.44 on August 26. Rasonque is currently approved only in the United States.

Pharma Industry.content:

Written by Eric Funderburk for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas)
Summary
GLP-1 drug production is driving billions of dollars' worth of pharmaceutical industry construction spending in the U.S. and the world.
A Big Market
The development and use of GLP-1 drugs to aid weight loss has been the biggest thing to hit the Pharmaceutical-Biotech Industry for some time. According to Industrial Info Resources data, GLP-1 drug production is driving billions of dollars' worth of construction in the U.S. and elsewhere.
Showing the extent of GLP-1 adoption in the U.S., the results of a Gallup News poll published in July found that the amount of U.S. adults taking GLP-1 drugs for weight loss purposes has risen to 11% in 2026, up from 3% in 2024. Fifteen percent of Americans reported using the drugs for weight loss at some point in their lives. The rapid adoption is even having a knock-on effect on the food and grocery sector, with a recent study led by Cornell University indicating that households with at least one GLP-1 user saw a 6% reduction in grocery bills within six months.
The makers of GLP-1 drugs, particularly the blockbusters that have nearly become household names, are putting their investment dollars to work at new and expanded plants both in and out of the U.S., accounting for billions of dollars' worth construction spending. While injectables continue to drive construction in a big way, so are the more recently developed oral GLP-1 doses in pill form.
Novo Nordisk
Novo Nordisk's Ozempic opened the door for GLP-1's used for weight loss and the company's popular Wegovy has gained prominence along with it. Novo Nordisk's U.S. manufacturing base is in Clayton, North Carolina, just on the edge of the state's famed Research Triangle, where it has had a presence since 1993. In 2020, Novo Nordisk completed a $2 billion expansion to manufacture active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) at the site, with an emphasis on insulin products. Industrial Info Resources reported on
the project
from 2015, before construction began, through its completion.
To expand its GLP-1 drug development, Novo Nordisk is now pouring another $4.1 billion into the Clayton campus, with its Ozempic and Wegovy offerings squarely in its sites. The massive project will roughly double Novo Nordisk's square footage in the state with 1.4 million square feet of additional building space. Readers can access details of the project, including construction timelines, key contact details, and equipment and service needs, by
clicking here
.
Serving a similar fill-finish purpose for Wegovy and Ozempic, in a 2024 deal worth $11 billion, Novo Nordisk acquired Catalent, a contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) with which the company already had ties, and its three fill-finish sites, including
a plant in Bloomington, Indiana
, and outside the U.S. in
Anagni, Italy
, and
Brussels, Belgium
.
Eli Lilly & Company
Already pouring billions of dollars into its
campus in Lebanon, Indiana
, Eli Lilly decided to further increase its investment as use of its tirzepatide GLP-1 drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound took off. According to Industrial Info Resources, Lilly is investing more than $13 billion in the site, which is inclusive of development and production of a larger range of products in addition to GLP-1s, although these feature prominently in its plans.
Even more related Eli Lilly projects are on the books--some with an emphasis on the company's up-and-coming oral orforglipron GLP-1 medication. Major orforglipron-related projects are on the books for
Houston, Texas
, where the company will produce small-molecule APIs for the GLP-1 oral drugs still needing regulatory authorization. Another project aimed at Lilly's oral-dose GLP-1 doses just broke ground in
Puerto Rico
, where a building addition is expected to begin contributing to oral-dose GLP-1 production in 2029. A
solar power array
will accompany the facility.
The new orforglipron drugs are also part of the company's plans to invest $6 billion in a grassroot campus in
Huntsville, Alabama
.
Eli Lilly's better-established injectable GLP-1 drugs Zepbound and Mounjaro--essentially the same drug, with Zepbound labeled specifically for weight loss and Mounjaro targeting diabetes, are a big part of the reason for a new
seven-building campus
in Fogelsville, in eastern Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley region, although its experimental weight-loss drug retatrutide, targeting additional pathways to GLP-1 drugs, also plays into the plans.
Novo Nordisk & Eli Lilly Outside of the U.S.
While Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly of course make other drugs in addition to GLP-1s, these types of drugs are factoring into Novo Nordisk's
US$9.1 billion worth of construction
presently underway outside of the U.S., with more on the books. Novo Nordisk's home country Denmark, where most of its construction outside of the U.S. is occurring, has one of the highest GLP-1 adoption rates in Europe, at about 9%, according to market research firm YouGov.
Industrial Info Resources is tracking
US$3.2 billion of Eli Lilly's international construction
happening at the moment, with another US$3.7 billion in various stages of planning and engineering. One of Lilly's most notable upcoming construction projects an
oral-dose GLP-1 plant in the Netherlands
on which the company plans to drop more US$1.5 billion, with the possibility of
doubling that investment in the future
.
Key Takeaways
GLP-1 drug production is driving billions of dollars of construction projects both inside and outside the U.S.
Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly & Company represent two of the highest spenders in this area, thanks to blockbuster weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound.
Up-and-coming oral dose GLP-1 drugs are gaining ground and driving new projects.
About Industrial Info Resources
Industrial Info Resources (IIR) is the leading provider of industrial market intelligence. Since 1983, IIR has provided comprehensive research, news and analysis on the industrial process, manufacturing and energy related industries. IIR's Global Market Intelligence (GMI) helps companies identify and pursue trends across multiple markets with access to real, qualified and validated plant and project opportunities. Across the world, Industrial Info Resources is tracking over 250,000 current and future projects worth $30.2 trillion (USD).

Good morning, everyone, and how are you today? We are doing just fine, thank you, despite the soggy weather hovering over the Pharmalot campus right now, because our spirits remain sunny, nonetheless. Why? We will trot out a bit of insight from the Morning Mayor, who would say “Every new day should be unwrapped like a precious gift.” To celebrate the notion, we are brewing still more cups of stimulation and invite you to join us. Our choice today is the mysterious witch’s brew. Meanwhile, here are a few items of interest. Hope you have a smashing day and, of course, do stay in touch. …
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a life-extending treatment for advanced pancreatic cancer made by Revolution Medicines that is the first to attack a genetic cause of the aggressive, highly lethal malignancy,
STAT
says. The approval was supported by a practice-changing clinical trial showing patients with advanced pancreatic cancer who received the drug as a second-line treatment achieved a median overall survival of 13.2 months, compared to 6.7 months for patients given standard chemotherapy.
Advertisement
The Trump administration plans to announce a new round of drug-pricing agreements with several midsized biotech companies on Monday
,
Bloomberg News
reports. The companies will agree to provide discounts on outpatient drugs to state Medicaid programs so that the prices states pay align with what the companies charge in foreign countries. Participation by state Medicaid programs is optional. In exchange, the companies will be exempt from pilot programs forcing similar discounts in Medicare. Relief from tariffs is also part of some of the discussions.

The company reports that the 2 year results add longer term context to earlier TransCon CNP findings for children with achondroplasia.

Ascendis Pharma is a US based biopharmaceutical company that develops TransCon based therapies for unmet medical needs, so the new achondroplasia data and approval sit within a broader effort to build a rare disease portfolio across Europe, the United States, and other markets.

YUVIWEL approval and 2 year TransCon CNP data reinforce Ascendis Pharma’s rare disease thesis
For investors following Ascendis Pharma, this update strengthens the existing narrative that TransCon based therapies can support a multi product rare disease portfolio. The Week 104 data in achondroplasia and US approval of YUVIWEL both relate directly to the catalyst around regulatory and commercial rollout of TransCon CNP in achondroplasia and potential use across growth indications. The news also partially addresses concerns that this third pillar of the portfolio might contribute less than hoped, although it does not remove execution risk on global launches or real world uptake.
If we take a look at the
community Narrative for Ascendis Pharma
, we can see how this news fits into the bigger investment story.
The key unresolved piece is how YUVIWEL and the broader TransCon CNP franchise convert into revenue. Investors may want to watch the next few quarterly reports through 2027 for disclosed YUVIWEL sales trends and commentary on patient starts and reimbursement, since those data points could play an important role in confirming or challenging the current TransCon growth story.

Overview

The pharmaceutical lipids market is emerging as a vital component of modern drug development, driven by the rising use of lipid-based delivery platforms, biologics, and advanced therapeutic technologies. Pharmaceutical lipids are widely used in formulations such as lipid nanoparticles, liposomes, lipid emulsions, and drug encapsulation systems to improve drug stability, bioavailability, and targeted delivery. Growing demand for RNA-based medicines, gene therapies, and injectable formulations is significantly increasing the adoption of specialized lipid ingredients.
Pharmaceutical
companies are investing heavily in advanced lipid systems, including ionizable lipids, phospholipids, and cholesterol-based carriers, to enhance treatment outcomes. Lipid-based formulations are also gaining importance in oncology, infectious disease treatment, and rare disease therapies due to their ability to provide controlled and targeted drug release.
North America continues to hold a significant position in the market due to strong
biotechnology
research activities, increasing
clinical trials
, and established pharmaceutical manufacturing capabilities.
Meanwhile, the Asia-Pacific is experiencing rapid growth supported by expanding healthcare infrastructure, rising drug production, and increasing investments in biopharmaceutical innovation. Ongoing advancements in lipid chemistry and personalized medicine are expected to create new opportunities for market expansion.

31.3%

Regional Analysis
In 2024, North America dominated the pharmaceutical lipids market, accounting for more than
33.5%
share with a market value of approximately
US$ 1.4 billion

The region’s growth was driven by increasing adoption of lipid-based drug delivery systems, rising demand for high-quality pharmaceutical excipients, and expanding research activities in advanced therapies. Strong biotechnology infrastructure and the presence of specialized manufacturing facilities supported efficient production of complex lipid formulations.
The region benefited from rapid advancements in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), particularly for mRNA-based therapies, oncology applications, and metabolic disease treatments. Increased clinical research, supportive regulatory frameworks, and collaborations between pharmaceutical companies and research institutions further strengthened market expansion.
Growing investments in personalized medicine and biologics manufacturing are expected to enhance future demand for pharmaceutical lipids. With continuous innovation, advanced
healthcare
infrastructure, and strong development capabilities, North America is projected to maintain its leading position in the global pharmaceutical lipids market.
Emerging Trends
Lipid Nanoparticles (LNPs) Becoming Key Drug Delivery Platforms:
Lipid nanoparticles are emerging as a major pharmaceutical lipid trend due to their ability to transport mRNA, RNA therapies, and genetic medicines. Research published in 2025 highlights that LNPs improve nucleic acid protection, cellular uptake, and delivery efficiency. Many LNP systems contain 4 major components: ionizable lipids, phospholipids, cholesterol, and PEG-lipids.
Rising Demand for mRNA-Based Therapeutics and Vaccines:
The expansion of mRNA medicine is increasing demand for specialized pharmaceutical lipids. FDA-reviewed vaccine platforms in 2026 continue using lipid nanoparticle technology for mRNA delivery. These systems enable rapid vaccine development by protecting mRNA molecules and supporting immune response generation with precise lipid formulations.
Growth of Liposomal Drug Formulations:
Liposomal formulations are gaining adoption for improving drug stability, reducing toxicity, and providing controlled release. Pharmaceutical lipids are widely used in oncology, antifungal, and targeted therapies. Advanced lipid carriers are being designed to improve drug loading capacity and enhance therapeutic performance through optimized lipid compositions.
Development of Targeted Lipid Delivery Systems
: Pharmaceutical companies and researchers are focusing on programmable lipid nanoparticles that deliver medicines to specific tissues. These systems are being explored for cancer treatment, gene therapy, and rare disease applications. New lipid designs aim to improve targeting accuracy, reduce side effects, and increase treatment effectiveness.
Advanced Manufacturing and Quality Control of Lipid Products:
Manufacturing innovation is becoming important for pharmaceutical lipid production as demand increases for complex therapies. Researchers are developing improved formulation methods, analytical tools, and scalable production approaches. These technologies help maintain lipid particle size, stability, and consistency during commercial drug manufacturing.
Use Cases
mRNA Vaccine Delivery Applications:
Pharmaceutical lipids are widely used as delivery vehicles for mRNA vaccines because they protect genetic material from degradation and support cellular absorption. FDA-reviewed mRNA vaccine technologies use lipid nanoparticles containing encapsulated mRNA, demonstrating the importance of lipids in next-generation preventive medicines.
Cancer Treatment and Oncology Drug Delivery:
Lipid-based drug delivery systems are increasingly used in cancer therapies to improve drug concentration at tumor sites. Liposomes and lipid nanoparticles help deliver chemotherapy agents, nucleic acids, and targeted molecules while potentially reducing exposure to healthy tissues and improving treatment safety.
Gene Therapy and RNA Therapeutics:
Pharmaceutical lipids support gene therapy development by enabling the delivery of RNA-based medicines such as mRNA and siRNA. LNP technology provides protection against enzymatic breakdown and improves intracellular transport. Research identifies lipid nanoparticles as leading non-viral carriers for nucleic acid therapeutics.
Controlled Drug Release Formulations
: Lipid-based carriers are used to create controlled-release medicines that maintain therapeutic levels for longer durations. Liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles, and related systems improve drug solubility and bioavailability. These applications support treatments requiring stable and sustained drug delivery profiles.
Personalized Medicine and Precision Healthcare:
Pharmaceutical lipids are supporting personalized medicine by enabling customized delivery systems based on patient-specific therapeutic needs. Researchers are developing adaptable lipid formulations for genetic diseases, immune therapies, and targeted treatments. Advanced lipid platforms aim to improve treatment precision while reducing unwanted biological effects.
Frequently Asked Questions on
Pharmaceutical Lipids
What is the pharmaceutical lipids market?
The pharmaceutical lipids market refers to the global industry involved in manufacturing, supplying, and developing lipid ingredients for pharmaceutical products. The market is expanding due to increasing demand for lipid-based drug delivery, biologics, vaccines, and RNA-based therapeutics across healthcare systems worldwide.
What factors are driving the pharmaceutical lipids market?
Growing use of lipid nanoparticles in RNA therapeutics, increasing biologic drug production, rising demand for poorly soluble drug formulations, and continuous innovation in drug delivery technologies are major growth drivers. Expanding pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity further supports market development globally.
Which types of pharmaceutical lipids are widely used?
Common pharmaceutical lipids include phospholipids, triglycerides, fatty acids, cholesterol, and specialized cationic or ionizable lipids. These materials are selected based on formulation needs, helping improve drug encapsulation, controlled release, bioavailability, and overall therapeutic performance in modern medicines.
How are pharmaceutical lipids used in drug delivery?
Pharmaceutical lipids form carriers such as liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles, and lipid nanoparticles that protect active ingredients and improve targeted delivery. These systems enhance drug stability, increase absorption, reduce toxicity, and enable controlled release for improved patient outcomes.
Which region leads the pharmaceutical lipids market?
North America currently leads the pharmaceutical lipids market because of its advanced pharmaceutical manufacturing infrastructure, strong biotechnology sector, significant investment in innovative drug development, and widespread adoption of lipid-based formulations for vaccines, biologics, and RNA therapeutics.
Who are the major end users of pharmaceutical lipids?
Major end users include pharmaceutical companies, biotechnology firms, contract development and manufacturing organizations (CDMOs), research institutes, and academic laboratories. These organizations utilize pharmaceutical lipids for drug formulation, clinical research, commercial manufacturing, and development of advanced therapeutics.
What is the future outlook for the pharmaceutical lipids market?
The pharmaceutical lipids market is expected to experience steady growth as demand increases for RNA therapeutics, personalized medicines, lipid nanoparticle technologies, and advanced biologic formulations. Ongoing innovation and expanding pharmaceutical production capacities are likely to create new opportunities worldwide.
Conclusion
The pharmaceutical lipids market is expected to witness steady growth as lipid-based drug delivery becomes increasingly important for biologics, vaccines, gene therapies, and advanced pharmaceutical formulations. Rising demand for improved drug solubility, bioavailability, and targeted delivery continues to support the adoption of high-purity pharmaceutical lipids across multiple therapeutic areas.
Triglycerides, plant-derived lipids, liposomes, and parenteral formulations remain key growth segments, while pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical companies account for the largest share of demand. Continued investments in lipid nanoparticle technologies, expanding biologics pipelines, and increasing research in precision medicine are expected to create new opportunities.
With strong manufacturing capabilities, regulatory support, and ongoing innovation, North America is expected to maintain its leadership, while Asia-Pacific is likely to emerge as a high-growth region. Overall, the market outlook remains positive, driven by technological advancements and the expanding role of lipid-based therapeutics in modern healthcare.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: Kazakhstan records surge in pharmaceutical investment in 2025 - trend.az
Pharma Industry.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 28.
Investment in
Kazakhstan's pharmaceutical industry increased by 56% in 2025,
reaching $142.8 million, the press service of the Government of
Kazakhstan said.
This was announced in a statement by the press service of the
Kazakh Government.
According to the information, a further $7.1 million was
attracted in the first quarter of 2026. Major international
pharmaceutical companies, including AstraZeneca, Pfizer and Roche,
are participating in projects aimed at localizing production and
transferring technologies to Kazakhstan.
"Under the instruction of the Head of State, eight major
projects are being implemented to establish and expand
pharmaceutical production facilities. Their launch will make it
possible to produce more than 494 types of medicines in Kazakhstan
for the first time," the statement said.
The projects will cover medicines for the treatment of cancer,
cardiovascular, autoimmune, orphan and infectious diseases, as well
as diabetes.
The government noted that the development of Kazakhstan's
pharmaceutical industry is proceeding in several areas, ranging
from expanding domestic production and localizing technologies to
improving access to medicines in the regions.
Overall, pharmaceutical production in Kazakhstan has increased
by 37% over the past three years, reaching 191 billion tenge (about
$416 million).
Kazakhstan is continuing to modernize its healthcare system,
with efforts focused on expanding domestic pharmaceutical
production, developing medical infrastructure in the regions,
addressing healthcare staffing shortages, and introducing digital
technologies.
The measures are being implemented as part of the instructions
given by Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in his Address to
the People of Kazakhstan, "Kazakhstan in the Era of Artificial
Intelligence: Current Challenges and Their Solutions Through
Digital Transformation."
The President has instructed the government to increase the
volume and range of domestically produced medicines and introduce
modern digital tools to monitor the quality and volume of
healthcare services.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: Korea’s biotechs pivot beyond ADCs, target toxicity cuts and delivery gains - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
Pharma Industry.content: Once hailed as a “next-generation anticancer drug” amid a fierce race to out-license technology, the Antibody-Drug Conjugate (ADC) is at a new crossroads, analysts said. The core of the next competition is not how many are developed, but who first overcomes the limits of current ADCs. At the 4th Samsung Medical Center·Aimed Bio Antibody-Drug Conjugate (ADC) Conference held at the Westin Seoul Parnas in Gangnam-gu, Seoul, on the 28th, Chair Nam Do-hyun Aimed Bio(0009K0), Chair Kim Yong-ju LigaChem Biosciences(141080), CEO Park Tae-gyo IntoCell(287840), CEO Lee Sang-hoon ABL Bio(298380), and CEO Lee Sung-joo Orum Therapeutics(475830) agreed that the base of Korea’s ADC industry has rapidly expanded over the past year. Chair Nam said, “This year, it has reached the point where it feels odd if a domestic pharma or biotech company is not doing ADC.” But as the industry has grown, competition has become more intense. This is no longer an era when business viability comes just from making one ADC. Companies need to find better targets, reduce toxicity, and develop technology that delivers drugs precisely to where they are needed. At the same time, they must consider how to expand beyond ADCs to next-generation therapeutic technologies. ◇ Round 2 of the ADC race… focus on linkers and payloads to cut toxicity The biggest limitation of current ADCs is toxicity. An ADC is a therapy that links a drug that kills cancer cells to an antibody that homes to cancer cells. In theory, because the antibody finds the cancer cell and delivers the drug, it can reduce the impact on normal cells. But in actual clinical settings, unanticipated hematologic toxicity and other adverse events often emerge, preventing sufficiently high dosing. Chair Kim Yong-ju said LigaChem Biosciences is strengthening efforts to analyze the correlation between in vivo drug exposure and toxicity by leveraging its large-scale clinical pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) data. The aim is to go beyond asking “which drug is effective” and use data to identify under what conditions toxicity appears. IntoCell CEO Park Tae-gyo said, “By mechanism, ADCs are targeted therapies, but the way currently made ADCs actually behave is as cytotoxic chemotherapies,” adding, “The technology has not advanced enough yet, which is why they are not being evaluated that way.” Cytotoxic chemotherapies broadly attack rapidly dividing cells, while targeted therapies aim at specific proteins or genetic alterations present in cancer cells. ADCs are largely composed of an antibody, linker, and payload. The antibody is the “guidance system” that homes to cancer cells, the linker connects the antibody and the drug and serves as the bridge that allows the drug to be released at the right time, and the payload is the anticancer component that actually kills cancer cells. Until now, ADC technology competition has focused on how precisely these three elements are combined. But there is growing sentiment that it is no longer easy to differentiate just by combining these elements. Chair Kim said, “The technology to conjugate a drug to an antibody is now something anyone can do,” adding, “By itself, it is hard to differentiate.” He continued, “To solve the innate problems of ADCs, we should focus more on linkers and payloads, which still have greater room for optimization.” As the ADC market expands, attempts to combine various technologies—such as bispecific antibodies or “dual payloads” that carry two types of anticancer agents—are also increasing. ABL Bio is a representative example. CEO Lee Sang-hoon said, “We are a company that, while developing antibodies, came to combine bispecific antibodies with ADCs,” adding, “We are currently studying whether leveraging the ability of bispecific antibodies to penetrate deep into tumor tissue can improve payload delivery efficiency.” Some urged caution. CEO Park said, “For ADCs, the antibody, linker, drug, and even the combinations of linkers and drugs each need to be optimized,” adding, “On top of that, stacking bispecifics or other elements to optimize every combination simultaneously is, in reality, far too complex.” In other words, just because a bispecific antibody homes to cancer cells better does not mean that attaching it to an ADC will yield an optimal therapy. Park said, “It is necessary to take on new technologies, but we must soberly assess the chances of success,” adding, “It is important to focus on the direction with the highest likelihood of success.” ◇ ADCs alone aren’t enough… “We look for the technology needed in five years” The discussion goes a step further: preparing for “what comes after ADCs.” Chair Kim Yong-ju said recent efforts at LigaChem Biosciences are widening the view beyond ADCs, adding, “We want to keep only what ADCs do well and change everything else.” For now, the focus is on how to deliver drugs. Kim said, “These days we are meeting many companies with diverse drug delivery technologies,” adding, “By changing formulations or using new carriers, there may be a chance to modulate in vivo exposure and reduce toxicity.” Orum Therapeutics is developing DACs that combine ADCs with targeted protein degradation (TPD) technology. CEO Lee Sung-joo said, “We were focused only on cancer drugs, but recently we started applying our technology to other areas,” adding, “When we said in 2019 that we would do DACs, many asked why we were doing that. Among the things people ask ‘why’ about now, we are constantly thinking about which technologies will be needed in five years.” CEO Lee Sang-hoon stressed that to do so, companies must closely watch changes in the external market. He said, “ABL Bio’s blood-brain barrier (BBB) shuttle technology and small interfering RNA (siRNA) research began that way,” adding, “In discussions with global pharma, we picked up signals that existing antibody technology alone might be insufficient, and we linked that to a new research direction.” All of this ultimately requires money. Although LigaChem Biosciences recently secured about 500 billion won through the Public Growth Fund, Chair Kim said he is actually “worried because there are too many places to spend it.” He said, “We are currently conducting multiple ADC clinical trials, and the number of programs entering the clinic continues to grow,” adding, “Once you run trials, you realize just how much money it takes.” Orum Therapeutics, which holds about 250 billion won in cash, also plans to invest most of it in developing new payloads and clinical research. CEO Lee Sung-joo said, “The reason we raised convertible preferred stock (CPS) at the end of last year was not because we immediately needed funds,” adding, “We secured capital with the mindset that when a good wave comes, you have to ride it.” There were also calls for investors to be more actively involved in the ADC industry. Chair Kim said, “ADC chemistry, manufacturing and controls (CMC) is ‘hell,’” adding, “Clinical physicians and investors must be at the table for these discussions.”
